title: Implement staged read-through cache with adaptive SWR to reduce Console aggregation load
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: Console backend continues to suffer from high CPU and DB read amplification on dashboard list/rollup endpoints. Multiple GraphQL clients fan out similar requests that bypass the existing TTL cache during bursts, creating repeated background aggregation runs and long tail 95-99th latency spikes. Current per-route TTLs are coarse and cause either stale data or cache stampedes.
approach: Introduce a staged read-through cache layer backed by Redis (as the primary fast read store) and a small in-process LRU tier for hot keys. Add adaptive stale-while-revalidate (SWR) semantics: when a key is expired but within an adaptive grace window, serve the stale payload synchronously while kicking an async background refresh. The grace window adapts based on recent QPS and observed refresh latency to balance freshness vs. thundering refreshes.
design_decisions: 1) Read-through vs write-through: choose read-through to avoid coupling all writers and to keep aggregation recompute logic centralized. 2) Two-tier cache: in-process LRU for micro-hot prefixes reduces mem allocations and network hops for extreme hotspots. 3) Freshness metadata: store last-fetched timestamp + ETag in Redis to allow conditional requests to downstream aggregators. 4) Fallback policy: if stale beyond hard threshold or background refresh fails repeatedly, fall back to realtime aggregator with circuit-breaker and exponential backoff.
tradeoffs:
- Serving slightly stale results reduces load but increases exposure to out-of-date dashboard numbers for a short period. We mitigate with conservative grace windows for high-SLA routes.
- Added complexity in cache invalidation and refresh orchestration. We simplify by restricting write invalidation to a small set of mutation paths and leverage existing webhook/event topics for targeted invalidation.
- Redis cost increases vs DB RPS reduction; justified by lower CPU and tail latency and improved request success rates.
implementation_notes:
- Redis schema: key -> {payload, last_fetched_iso, etag, refresh_attempts}.
- Background refresh worker: pool sized by route QPS; uses token bucket to limit refresh concurrency.
- Adaptive grace algorithm: grace = min(max_base + alpha * recent_qps, max_grace_ms).
- Instrumentation: expose metrics for cache_hit, cache_stale_served, refresh_success_rate, refresh_latency_p50/p95/p99, refresh_concurrency, db_reads_saved.
- API changes: none; behavior controlled by feature flag 'staged_cache_swr' and route-level config in console-config service.
rollout_plan:
1) Merge behind feature flag. 2) Canary 5% of traffic (internal console only) for 48h; monitor refresh success and 95th latency. 3) Expand to 25% for 72h; run a synthetic E2E suite exercising common dashboards. 4) 100% if metrics stable. 5) If regressions observed, rollback to previous flag state and investigate.
Health gates: p95 latency should not increase by >10% from baseline, cache_hit_ratio should improve on targeted routes, DB RPS should drop by >=25% for those routes.
testing_plan:
- Unit tests for cache read/write and metadata handling.
- Integration tests with a Redis test double and a mocked aggregator.
- Load test scenario mimicking top 50 console queries to validate reduced backend aggregation jobs.
- Chaos test: kill background refresh workers to verify fallback and circuit-breaker.
- Canary monitoring and automated alerting: Slack alarm if refresh_success_rate < 95% or refresh_latency_p99 spikes >2x.
metrics_and_dashboards:
- Console: console.cache.hit_ratio, console.cache.stale_served, console.cache.refresh_latency_p95, console.backend.p95_latency, console.backend.cpu_utilization, db.read_rps.
- Dashboard links: https://grafana.internal.redwood/company/console-cache-overview (canary panel), https://grafana.internal.redwood/company/console-backend-hotpaths
risks_and_mitigation:
- Risk: cache poisoning or stale critical data. Mitigation: for high-sensitivity routes (billing, security audit logs) SWR disabled and we rely on strict TTL + invalidation.
- Risk: background refresh storms. Mitigation: global token bucket and jittered backoff, plus per-key refresh_attempts cap.
- Risk: operational complexity. Mitigation: start with 2-3 highest-impact routes, add runbook and dashboarding before broader rollout.
